title: The Heart of What Was Lost
author: Tad Williams
review:
4.5/5

This book is incredibly well done, Tad Williams adds a lot of flavor to his world and poses a lot of moral questions on the nature of what should be done in the aftermath of a war against a seemingly unforgiving enemy. I would agree with criticism of Tad's previous books in the series in that they tend to be longer than they really should be, but here he proves that he can write a great story with a leaner page count and it doesn't lose any of his signature prose or world building.

“The Dance of What Will Be. It is going on all around us and inside us. It seems to follow a set course of steps, but in truth there is no fixed pattern.” Isgrimnur scowled. “In other words, you don’t know if we can knock the gate down.”
“We are already dead and our ends sung! Let what we have already lost bring freedom to those we loved! For the Queen and the Garden!”

“‘Do you think when we meet someday in the Garden that I could face the shade of my great foreparent, our queen’s consort, if I laid down my arms and let the mortals have their way? Do you think I could bear his gaze if I knew that I had let fear make me a weak thing?

“I think your kind are little better than animals,” she said at last, “But I think you are an honest mortal. That does not mean I would not happily kill you and tie your head to my saddle by that bristling beard.”
“We have all done strange things here at the ends of the earth.”
Dark, thought Viyeki. It is always so dark inside the mountain and inside the hearts of the Hikeda’ya.

“Suno’ku was the heart of what was lost, but made flesh—one who believed the old truths with all her spirit, and could make them real to others by the force of her own belief. But the old truths, I fear, are no longer true, Viyeki-tza. That is why the next generation will require different minds, different truths.

He had come to the order-house prepared to die. But what if he did not? How could he live each day from now on knowing that all he had thought simple and true was instead as tangled and foul as the roots of a rotting tree?

He had left the house empty, a man who thought himself already dead. Now he was something else—a man who, as his master had said, could see around corners. A man who could think about the days still to come.
